units.translation: 212-14a. You truly: the verb "are" is missing. The sense is: my mind still knows each thing through my prophetic art. By this he does nothing other than, while professing his skill, secretly summon them to an alliance.
b. A favor to you, O lord: I return thanks to you even though I am in misfortunes.

215-216a. Whoever is most terrible: whoever is fearful to those who sin against suppliants. Properly, with regard to the circumstances, he mentions not Zeus Xenios but Zeus Hikesios, since he himself is as a suppliant of the heroes because of his pressing need.
b. And around Phoebus: this he says either as a prophet or because the god has become the cause of the voyage.
218. Aid me: help me. For the Cleitorians say "chraismein" for "to assist." It is declined from the barytone "chraismō," as "bainō bainete"; for the perispomenon is "chraismeite."
221. Unwound: it is also written "amēryon," that is, unaccomplished
and continually enduring, endless. Or not having an end; he means not having death. The metaphor is from wool being wound.

222-24a. And besides most bitter: wishing to increase the pathos, he began from the suffering itself. The sense is: in addition to the other evils, another most bitter one hangs over one after another. "Unspeakable" means unrecognizable, unforeseen, unclear.
b. There are three Harpies: Celaeno, Ocypete, and Aello. BPa
225-27a. "I hold:" I have. Lg
b. But quickly: so swiftly they come from the unseen. He has used "his own" badly, saying it instead of "my."
c. Caring: taking thought. This he said divinely. For he did not say "feasting" or "eating," but only having thought for food, in order to heighten the pathos.
231. Wrought: instead of "forged." Adamant is both a stone and a kind of hard iron.
232-33. But bitter and insatiate: the much-harming one. This for greater emphasis, as if not only to bear the smell, but also to remain steadfastly because of blindness.
234. It is fated for them: it is destined that the Harpies be killed by the Boreads. He used "thesphaton" as if very necessarily, as things happening by compulsion.

235. Nor strangers: being not strangers to me, they will help. That kinship makes everyone more eager for good deeds, Euripides also says (Or. 486): "It is Greek to honor always those from the same place."
238-39. Their sister: Cleopatra, daughter of Boreas and Oreithyia, sister of Zetes and Calais, whom Phineus married. Their children were Parthenius and Carambis.
240. "He was:" he said. Lg
241. And around two: perhaps he says that the Boreads pity him more because of kinship.
243. Being distressed: being troubled. Lg P
244a. "More grievous:" more toilsome. Lg
